text: Your body is about sixty percent water, and it loses some every single minute, even while you sleep.
So what actually happens, hour by hour, if you stop drinking completely?
Let's start with the numbers.
In an average adult, water makes up roughly fifty to sixty percent of body weight.
Most of it sits inside your cells. The rest flows in your blood and between your tissues.
Water carries nutrients, removes waste, cushions your joints, and keeps your temperature stable.
In other words, almost everything your body does depends on it.
And that share changes with age.
A newborn baby is around seventy-five percent water.
With age, the share tends to fall, because older bodies usually carry less muscle, and muscle holds a lot of water.
Your brain and your heart are each roughly three quarters water.
Your bones, surprisingly, still contain around a fifth to a third.
And you are losing it all the time.
You breathe out water vapor with every breath.
Your skin releases water, even when you do not feel sweaty.
And your kidneys produce urine to flush out waste.
Even resting in a cool room, an adult typically loses around two and a half liters a day.
In heat, or during exercise, that can double, or more.
Sweat is your built-in air conditioner.
When sweat evaporates from your skin, it carries heat away with it.
During hard exercise in hot weather, a person can lose more than a liter of sweat in a single hour.
That is why people working or running in the heat can get dehydrated surprisingly fast, long before they feel it.
And every liter of sweat also takes salt with it.
Hour one. You probably feel nothing.
But your brain is already watching.
Special sensors detect that your blood is becoming slightly more concentrated.
Once you have lost around one to two percent of your body weight in water, you start to feel thirsty.
At the same time, your brain releases a hormone called vasopressin, which tells your kidneys to save water.
Your urine becomes smaller in volume, and darker in color.
Hour eight.
Your mouth feels dry. You may feel tired, and a little irritable.
Several studies suggest that losing just two percent of your body water can make it harder to concentrate, and can lower your physical performance.
Some people get a headache.
Your body is still coping, but it is clearly sending you a message.
Hour twenty-four.
Now your blood volume starts to drop.
Less blood means less pressure, so your heart beats faster to keep everything supplied.
You sweat less, which makes it harder to cool down.
Your skin feels dry, and you may feel dizzy when you stand up too quickly.
But here's where it gets strange.
Thirst is not a perfect alarm.
As people get older, the feeling of thirst often becomes weaker.
That is one reason older adults are at higher risk of dehydration, especially during heat waves.
They can be short of water without feeling truly thirsty.
Day two.
Your kidneys are now working hard to keep as much water as possible, and you produce very little urine.
Muscle cramps, nausea and a pounding headache become common.
Your body starts to prioritize: blood flow is directed toward the most vital organs, like the brain and the heart.
Day three.
This is the danger zone.
When water losses reach around ten percent of body weight, confusion and delirium can set in.
The kidneys can start to fail, and waste builds up in the blood.
Losses of fifteen to twenty percent are often fatal. At this stage, this is a medical emergency.
You may have heard the survival rule of three: three minutes without air, three days without water, three weeks without food.
It is a rough guide, not a law.
In a hot desert, under the sun, a person can be in serious danger in much less time.
Resting in a cool place, some people have survived longer.
One famous case comes from Austria, in nineteen seventy-nine.
A young man was put in a holding cell, and then forgotten.
He reportedly survived around eighteen days, partly by licking condensation from the walls.
It is an extreme exception, and it shows how hard the body fights to survive.
And what about the champions of thirst?
Many people think a camel stores water in its hump.
It does not. The hump is mostly fat, a reserve of energy.
The real trick is elsewhere: camels can lose a large share of their body water and keep going, and their red blood cells are specially shaped to handle it.
When a very thirsty camel finally finds water, it can drink around one hundred liters in a matter of minutes.
Now, a common misconception.
Many people believe everyone must drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
In reality, there is no single magic number.
Your needs depend on your size, the weather, and how active you are.
And a good part of your water comes from food: fruit, vegetables, soup.
Drinks like tea and coffee also count toward your daily water.
So how much do you need?
European health authorities suggest around two liters of total water a day for women, and two and a half liters for men, including the water in food.
A simple clue is the color of your urine.
Pale yellow usually means you are well hydrated. Dark yellow often means you need to drink.
And here is the final twist.
Drinking far too much water in a short time can also be dangerous.
It can dilute the sodium in your blood, a condition called hyponatremia.
It is rare, but it has been seen in endurance athletes who drink much more than they sweat.
Balance is what your body wants.
So, without water: within hours, thirst and dark urine.
After one day, headache and a racing heart.
After about three days, real danger.
